title: Commit concurrent Future completion atomically against cancellation
applies_when: A cross-thread adapter returns a concurrent.futures.Future that remains cancellable while a synchronous or asynchronous callable executes, then checks cancelled() before writing its result or exception.
lesson: A cancelled() observation is not a reservation: another thread can cancel between that check and set_result/set_exception. Inspect both completion paths and their enclosing task group; an InvalidStateError can cancel unrelated portal work. The stdlib executor primitive set_running_or_notify_cancel() provides an atomic transition, normally before work starts. The accepted AnyIO repair instead uses it only when the adapter's callable has finished, not when it starts, to retain running-task cancellation. This is adapter-specific, not a general executor recipe. Exercise a real Future at the commit boundary, delegating to original state-changing methods instead of fabricating cancellation states. A controlled second thread works, but the maintainer-preferred regression is simpler: a Future subclass calls cancel() immediately before super().set_result/set_exception. This exposes the old race without another cancellation thread or redundant sync/async parametrization. Both a completed value and an accepted cancellation may be legitimate winners; neither should break the portal. Retain pre-completion cancellation and original exception delivery controls.
avoid_when: Do not apply this exact primitive to asyncio.Future, Promise, arbitrary awaitables or a caller-owned Future without checking their protocols. Moving the RUNNING transition to task start would disable the portal's supported running-task cancellation. Rechecking cancelled() alone leaves another race; tests that replace the state machine with a mock can hide it. Historical matched local evidence covers Windows/Linux CPython 3.12, asyncio variants and Trio: 16 regressions fail before the repair, with 230 passes, 4 skips and 1 existing xfail on the repaired thread modules. Those counts precede the maintainer-requested test simplification; they are not merged-head results. The start_blocking_portal context manager does not expose every background main-task exception; use the public async BlockingPortal when asserting task-group survival. Local optional Blockbuster and full pre-commit were not run in that qualification. Public CI covers its own configured matrix, not every optional combination. The merge establishes acceptance of this repair, not proof that next-evidence selection improves cost, recall or conversion.

evidence.note: Documents an executor/test-only transition normally called before executing work. The post-callable use in this particular cancellable adapter is an explicit lifecycle adaptation, not an instruction from the docs or a portable default.
Pinned baseline has check-then-write on both exception and normal completion. Its cancellation handler already uses the stdlib executor primitive, but these other paths do not.

Merged as 633965bad02a857574b3dbad03d1ef9f35e9caa4 after maintainer approval and regression simplification. The merged implementation retains the atomic transition on both value and exception paths; its RacingFuture test delegates to the real stdlib methods. Earlier native Windows/Linux and public CI evidence remains revision-specific. Retrospective Scout lead plus owner verification, not a preregistered selector comparison.
Earlier merged fix addresses cancellation callback registration, not result/exception completion. Similar cancellation wording does not establish identical ownership or mechanism.

Known-case Windows CPython3.12 native completeness calibration: the unchanged baseline fails all 16 sync/async/backend completion regressions; an authored result-only partial repair passes 8 but still fails all 8 exception cases; the full fix passes 16. The partial is a deliberate mutation, not an upstream revision. A success-only test would accept this incomplete fix. No model/selector utility or general mutation-detection rate is established.
